book: 100 - Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_

chapters.relation: The editor's introduction reframes the Batman-versus-Superman brawl: what fans are really arguing about is not strength but who is the better hero and "who should we try to be like." Michaud recalls learning sacrifice and persistence from Burton's Batman and total self-giving from the Death of Superman, and frames the book's choice as hope in humanity versus cynical vigilance about what people could become. He promises that the assembled philosophers flatly disagree and leaves the verdict of the fight to the reader.

chapters.file: ch08 - Pre-Fight Warm-Up Battle of the Billennium.md
ch09 - 1. Where Have All the Supermen Gone.md
chapters.relation: Holdier argues that neither hero is Nietzsche's Übermensch: Superman's servile mild-mannered Clark Kent guise would strike Nietzsche as slave morality, while Batman's self-loathing (his Hush confession that deep down he is not a good person) and breakable human body disqualify him too. Instead, reading them through The Birth of Tragedy and Grant Morrison's Supergods, Superman embodies the Apollonian force of order, sunlight, and rationality and Batman the Dionysian force of chaos and passion, so their battles (The Dark Knight Returns, Batman v Superman) are the inevitable but never-final friction of art's twin poles. The fight's real winner is the reader, who gets both deities at once.

chapters.file: ch10 - Round One Decision—Superman! The Son Shines Bright.md

chapters.relation: Malloy asks whether the two law-breaking vigilantes are criminals and whether any duty to obey the law survives scrutiny. He runs consent theory through Superman surrendering in handcuffs in Man of Steel and the Red Son Superman's residence in the USSR, uses Darkseid's Apokolips as Hobbes's security sovereign against Locke's natural-rights limits, deploys Hume against tacit consent (Batman would never leave Gotham even in No Man's Land), and dismantles gratitude theory (the Kents' adoption involved a sacrificial choice the law cannot make) and fair play (Nozick's Batman-lottery undercuts "I'm not wearing hockey pads"). He lands near Wolff-style philosophical anarchism: Superman's constrained lawbreaking endorses the law's legitimacy while Batman treats law as one more tool in his war, making him a force of chaos.

Springett applies evolutionary biology to the matchup: comparing fitness, adaptations, and arms races (Batman's escalating gadget war with his rogues versus Superman facing no competition at all), he concludes Superman is objectively fitter, while on the technical definition of altruism Batman is more altruistic than the invulnerable Superman, who cannot lower his own fitness. Redefining a "Superhero" as an individual who effectively raises the fitness of many others, and adding Gould's catastrophist view that species extinction is the norm, he argues a planet with Superman keeps the whole species alive through catastrophes Batman could never avert. He explicitly rejects Social Darwinism - Superman is its counterexample because he saves the less fit - and, with Dawkins, credits conscious awareness with letting us choose our own goals, crowning Superman the superior Superhero.

chapters.file: ch13 - 4. A Cape and a Code.md
chapters.relation: Farrell traces the heroes' knightly nicknames (Dark Knight, Caped Crusader, Man of Steel) to medieval chivalry as C.S. Lewis defines it in "The Necessity of Chivalry": the knight's double demand to be both stern and meek, each "to the nth degree," with knightly character a work of art achieved rather than a gift of nature. Both heroes show the split (playboy Bruce versus Spartan Batman in Batman Begins, meek Clark versus bold Superman), and both go to extremes - Batman's interrogation-room brutality in The Dark Knight, Superman turning back time for Lois in Superman: The Movie - but Lewis's hardest test is the mighty man who restrains himself. Superman's lifelong self-restraint, contrasted with uninhibited red-kryptonite Clark in Smallville's "Red," makes him the truer modern knight.

LaBauve opens with a staged Justice League debate over rescuing the Joker's hostages, where Batman's emotional, vengeance-tinged appeal loses to Superman's trust-based plea, and reads it through Aristotle's On Rhetoric: Batman persuades almost entirely by pathos (the relatable brokenness of Nolan's trilogy) with detective's logos, while Superman balances pathos, logos, and above all ethos, since Aristotle calls the speaker's character the strongest appeal. Against Max Landis's claim that Superman is irrelevant, he pairs the Death of Superman with Nietzsche's "God is dead" parable and the Kill Bill monologue to argue that Superman is a mythology of virtue - alongside real moral heroes like Gandhi, King, and Jesus - showing humans the ideal they ought to become, so Superman not only wins but must win.

chapters.file: ch15 - Round Two Decision—Batman! More Human than a Superman.md
ch16 - 6. The God We Need Now.md
chapters.relation: Ketcham stages the essay as a 1939 diary (a boyhood piece longing for a new god now that the biblical God has, he feels, abandoned the Depression-era world) followed by an old man's reread: America made Superman its messiah - born in a flash of light like the star of Bethlehem, canonized by DC's "publishing synod" much as the church redacted the New Testament - but he suspects the god will age as badly as the God of Abraham. Rereading after Korea, Vietnam, and Wall Street scandals, he argues we now need and worship a darker god modeled on Hades: the rich, hidden, vengeful billionaire Bruce Wayne, whose subterranean mansion, Cerberus-like Alfred, and tax-break tributes from citizens mirror the underworld god and Greek sacrifice. He ends imagining our grandchildren's next god as a cyber-god of AI, and declares Batman, not Superman, the god we need now.

chapters.file: ch17 - 7. How Batman Cowed a God.md
chapters.relation: Reider reads the two heroes through Nietzsche's genealogy of morals: Superman's humility, guilt, empathy, and farmer-parent values (he is Clark Kent at heart, keeping the alter ego to unload the burden of his power) are textbook slave morality, making him the unwitting pawn of the weak rather than Nietzsche's Übermensch, while Batman's pride, wrath, and vow of vengeance - he refuses to kill the Joker or Robin's attacker not from respect for life but from aristocratic pride - revive the pagan "good" of Achilles dragging Hector's body. From this he builds a deliberately provocative strategic claim: because slave morality leaves Superman secretly craving to be bested and made ordinary again, the merely human Batman can stare down and "cow" the god in their showdowns, winning the psychological war Wonder Woman's and Lois's preferences supposedly confirm.

Malloy uses the two heroes to explain supererogation - Urmson's "Saints and Heroes" puzzle of acts that are praiseworthy but not obligatory, like Batman rushing into burning buildings while Jimmy Olsen is under no duty to follow. Against the utilitarian and deontological denials that anything goes beyond duty (Singer's argument that Clark Kent's designer glasses are money he owes to charity, and Susan Wolf's Loving and Rational Saints whose lives, like Batman's broken retirements in The Dark Knight Returns and Batman Beyond, leave no room for anything worth living), he adopts Raz's view that a duty can be overridden by the moral reason of grave personal risk. Hence Batman's nightly risk-taking is a genuinely heroic choice, while Superman's powers make saving others morally required - so Batman is more truly a hero and Superman "just a good person with the powers of a living god."

Dupree and Fuš build an independent definition of the "true superhero" from identity statements (Batman = Bruce Wayne, Clark Kent = Superman): only an essentially human character who forges near-superhuman excellence through cultivated virtue can count, and Aristotle's virtue ethics supplies the standard. Batman qualifies - his refusal to kill the Joker shows the struggle for the golden mean between foolhardiness and cowardice, and Gotham Knights #31 shows how far he plans to avoid killing - whereas powers merely given, Superman's Kryptonian biology or the Green Lantern ring (their update of Gyges's Ring), bestow no virtue, as Kyle Rayner's and Guy Gardner's early careers show. Since Clark Kent is "in his heart" the alien Superman while Bruce Wayne is merely Batman's mask, Batman is a true superhero and Superman is not.

Michaud grants that Superman is godlike and turns Hume's problem of evil on him: if Superman is all-powerful, all-knowing, and good, why does suffering persist that he could prevent at super-speed - the desert animal dying painfully for no purpose, the crimes that happen while he picnics with Lois - and the free-will defense and "it's all part of the plan" excuses fail him even worse than they fail God. Superman then becomes our excuse for doing nothing, and like belief in immortality and the afterlife (holy wars where no one "really" dies, prayers instead of feeding the starving) he dulls our sense that this life is all we get. Reading Nietzsche's "God is dead" as the discovery that we keep gods only to feel special and saved, Michaud concludes we would live more meaningful, Batman-like self-reliant lives if the savior-Superman were dead to us.

chapters.file: ch21 - Round Three Decision—Superman! The Best Man for Tomorrow.md

chapters.relation: Springett argues Superman, not Batman, is the proper goal of transhumanism - Batman's training and gadgets are only a stage toward transcending the human condition - and that the eugenics and Social Darwinism objection fails because Superman directs his superior fitness at saving the less fit. Through Merleau-Ponty's embodied cognition (Lois's churning stomach over a deadline, Alfred retracing his steps and posture to recall a thought, the "Subway Superman" Wesley Autrey's instinctive track rescue) he shows that radically different bodies mean radically different minds and moral perception. That turns Nagel's "What Is It Like to Be a Bat?" into "what is it like to be Superman?" - a problem of other minds for our transhuman future, with Watchmen's Doctor Manhattan as the warning of a transcendent being who simply stops caring about humans.

In a fictional Dust Bowl voice, Ketcham has a 1940 farm kid watching foreclosure bulldozers decide which single comic hero to keep as the vigilante who will burn down the bank - weighing Superman, who has gone over to the big-city bankers as reporter Clark Kent, against Batman, whose riches resemble the bankers' but whose hatred of his parents' killer matches his own. He tests his candidates against Hamlet's fatal indecision, Henry V at Agincourt, a Lex Luthor who is evil exactly like the bank president, and Tom Joad of The Grapes of Wrath, the real "I'll be ever'where in the dark" vigilante. In the end the boy burns the Batman box, reads Superman's restraint as the preacher's forgiveness, and lets his anger - and the need for any vigilante - go.

Goldberg and Gavaler read the heroes' first-year comics (The Superman Chronicles, The Batman Chronicles) as rival moral codes: Superman is a "super consequentialist" out to benefit mankind - reforming the Blakely Mine owner, demolishing slums, buying back swindled stock - while Batman is a "dark deontologist" whose vengeance oath makes consequences irrelevant, waiting out the Joker's murders of Claridge, Wilde, and Judge Drake because catching the villain, not saving victims, is his duty. Mill's utilitarianism frames Superman's consequentialism and Kant's Groundwork - intentions over outcomes, the batarang blocked by invisible glass leaving Batman's morality untouched - frames Batman's, with moral luck the battleground: deontology shrugs it off, but Superman's powers let him smooth luck over too. On the opening dilemma, Superman defuses the bomb while Batman chases the villain, so the authors judge Superman's code superior because Batman's can let hundreds die without moral failure.

holes.name: Natural Selection (survival of the fittest)
holes.what: Darwin's mechanism of evolution: heritable variation plus differential survival and reproduction makes traits that fit an environment spread through a population.
holes.why: Chapter 12 measures Batman and Superman by fitness, adaptations, arms races, and biological altruism, and the taxonomy's social-darwinism slug covers only the ideology the chapter explicitly rejects, not the evolutionary framework it argues with.

holes.name: C.S. Lewis
holes.what: Twentieth-century Christian writer and medievalist whose essay "The Necessity of Chivalry" defines the knightly ideal as holding ferocity and meekness together to the nth degree.
holes.why: Chapter 13 evaluates Batman and Superman's knighthood entirely through Lewis's chivalry essay, and no taxonomy philosopher covers him.

holes.name: Ethos, Pathos, and Logos (On Rhetoric)
holes.what: Aristotle's three modes of persuasion in On Rhetoric: appealing to the speaker's character, to the audience's emotions, and to logic and facts.
holes.why: Chapter 14's entire argument ranks Batman and Superman as persuaders by how each balances the three modes, and no existing taxonomy slug names the rhetorical triad.

holes.name: Supererogation (beyond the call of duty)
holes.what: Actions that are praiseworthy to perform but not wrong to omit - the deeds of saints and heroes that go beyond obligation.
holes.why: Chapter 18 is built on supererogation from Urmson to Raz to decide whether Batman's risk-taking is heroic while Superman's rescues are mere duty, and the taxonomy has no slug for it.
